title: Medicaid coverage of doula care by state
methodology: We built this in October 2026. We started from the National Health Law Program's Doula Medicaid Project chart (updated September 2026) and the National Academy for State Health Policy's March 2026 analysis, then checked every state that covers doulas, or is working on it, against the state Medicaid agency's own documents: federally approved state plan amendments, provider manuals and bulletins, fee schedules and rules. Where those sources disagree, we use the state's own documents and explain the difference in the state's notes. A state is 'covered' when Medicaid is paying doulas now, 'enacted' when coverage is approved but payments haven't started, and 'pending' when rate-setting, rules or legislation are in progress. The maximum payment is the most Medicaid pays one doula for the standard package of prenatal and postpartum visits plus labor and delivery support, before extra visits that need prior approval and incentive payments; where vaginal and cesarean births pay differently, we show the higher amount. Medicaid pays the doula directly, so a mom on Medicaid pays nothing. Where a state bills by time with no cap, leaves rates to health plans, or doesn't publish rates, we show no total. Rates change often, usually on January 1 or July 1, so check with your state Medicaid agency or health plan before you count on a number.

fieldGuide.status: covered = Medicaid is paying doulas now; enacted = law or SPA approved, not yet paying; pending = rate-setting, rules or legislation in progress; not-covered = no benefit
fieldGuide.totalPaymentMax: most Medicaid pays one doula per pregnancy for the standard package, before prior-authorization extras and incentives; higher of vaginal/cesarean; null when time-billed with no cap, plan-negotiated, unpublished or unconfirmed

coverageCount.text: 28 states and DC pay doulas through Medicaid as of October 9, 2026. 3 more have approved coverage that isn't paying yet (NE, NH, VT), and 2 are working on it (ME, MT).

crossChecks.note: NASHP's count is as of March 2026 and covers statewide benefits under a state plan amendment. Since then Utah's benefit began (April 1, 2026) and Arkansas's (September 1, 2026); Florida's coverage is through health plans, not a SPA.

federalBasis.text: There is no federal requirement for Medicaid to cover doulas; each state chooses. States add doula care through a Medicaid state plan amendment (SPA) approved by CMS, and can also use a Section 1115 waiver, but the National Academy for State Health Policy (NASHP) found every state with a doula benefit uses a SPA. All of them cover doulas under the preventive services benefit, 42 CFR 440.130(c), which covers services recommended by a physician or other licensed practitioner. A 2013 CMS rule (78 FR 42160) changed that definition so non-licensed providers such as doulas can deliver preventive services when a licensed practitioner recommends them. That is why most states require a recommendation; NASHP counts 8 states with a statewide standing recommendation, so moms there don't need an individual referral.

laborDeliveryPaymentRange.text: Medicaid pays $459 to $1,500 for doula support during labor and delivery, depending on the state (NASHP, March 2026).

totalPaymentRange.text: Among covered states with a fixed per-pregnancy maximum, the standard doula package pays from $933.20 (AR) to $4,321.70 (DC). DC's figure is a theoretical cap built from long time-billed postpartum visits; the next highest caps are Washington ($3,500) and New Mexico ($3,300). Some states have no fixed maximum because visits are billed by time with no cap (Arizona, Illinois), rates are set by health plans (Florida), rates aren't published (Oklahoma, Utah, Virginia), or the visit limit couldn't be confirmed (Minnesota).

national.notes: Many Medicaid members are in managed care plans: a doula has to be in your plan's network, and plans can add their own rules. Most states also require a recommendation from a doctor, midwife or other licensed provider unless the state has issued a standing recommendation.

AZ.summary: In Arizona, Medicaid (AHCCCS) covers doula care with no visit limit: $16.28 per 15 minutes for prenatal and postpartum visits and $781.32 for labor and delivery, with a provider referral.
AZ.paymentNotes: $16.28 per 15 minutes for prenatal and postpartum visits (T1032, up to 2 hours / 8 units per day without prior authorization) and a flat $781.32 for labor and delivery (T1033, once per 9 months). Rates unchanged for FFY25, FFY26 and FFY27 (effective 10/1/2026). There is no cap on the number of visits, so there is no fixed per-pregnancy maximum.
AZ.certificationRequired: Arizona Dept. of Health Services (ADHS) state doula certification (national/other certifications alone do not qualify), then registration as an AHCCCS provider
AZ.notes: There's no visit limit: AHCCCS sets no minimum or maximum number of visits, and the 2-hours-per-visit and once-per-9-months labor limits can be exceeded with prior authorization, so there's no fixed per-pregnancy total. All pregnant or postpartum AHCCCS members qualify (no high-risk requirement) during pregnancy and up to one year postpartum, but a referral from an AHCCCS-registered provider (physician, midwife, NP, PA, and several behavioral health and clinic provider types) is required; there is no statewide standing recommendation. Health plans may not require prior authorization for doula services. Doulas serving managed-care members must also credential and contract with each AHCCCS health plan. AHCCCS has no member page about doulas; ask your health plan.
AZ.researchNotes: Matches NHeLP. No visit limit: AMPM 410 says there is no minimum or maximum number of visits, and the per-visit 2-hour and once-per-9-months L&D limits can be exceeded with prior authorization based on medical necessity, so totalPaymentMax is null. All pregnant or postpartum AHCCCS members qualify (no high-risk requirement) during pregnancy and up to one year postpartum, but a referral from an AHCCCS-registered provider (physician, midwife, NP, PA, and several behavioral health and clinic provider types) is required; there is no statewide standing recommendation. Health plans may not require prior authorization for doula services. Doulas serving managed-care members must also credential and contract with each AHCCCS health plan. AR.summary: In Arkansas, Medicaid covers doula care: up to $933.20 per pregnancy for 6 prenatal and postpartum visits, plus support during labor and delivery.
AR.paymentNotes: $64.45 per prenatal/postpartum visit (minimum 60 minutes; up to 6 combined) plus one flat labor and delivery payment that depends on the type of birth: $468.55 vaginal, $325.45 cesarean, $527.78 vaginal birth after a prior cesarean (VBAC), $546.50 cesarean after an attempted VBAC. Standard-package totals: $855.25 (vaginal), $712.15 (cesarean), $914.48 (VBAC), $933.20 (cesarean after attempted VBAC, the highest). Rates are from the DHS Supportive Maternal Care fee schedule (run 08/27/26). More than 6 visits only through a DHS extension of benefits.
AR.certificationRequired: Arkansas Dept. of Health Certified Community-Based Doula certification (through the Doula Alliance of Arkansas or another ADH-designated certifying organization; $50 fee), age 18+, NPI
AR.notes: Brand-new benefit. CMS approved SPA AR-26-0004 on July 22, 2026, with a retroactive effective date of March 1, 2026, but DHS opened doula enrollment and billing on September 1, 2026 (Official Notice ON-049-26; provider manual sections dated 9-1-26), so 2026-09-01 is used as the practical start. DHS also pays for labor support at a VBAC (vaginal birth after cesarean) or a cesarean after an attempted VBAC. Eligibility: pregnant or within 16 weeks postpartum; not enrolled in a Life360 HOME program; not already getting community health worker services from a CHW employed by an OB clinic. DHS obtained a statewide standing recommendation, so moms do not need a separate referral. The first visit must be in person and at least one visit must be in the mom's home; later prenatal/postpartum visits may be telehealth; labor support must be in person and not at home. No prior authorization for the standard 6 visits plus birth. Doulas who are also certified nurse-midwives cannot bill both for the same pregnancy. Arkansas DHS has no page for Medicaid members about the doula benefit yet.

CA.summary: In California, Medicaid covers doula care: up to $3,263.31 per pregnancy for an initial visit, 8 prenatal or postpartum visits and 2 extended postpartum visits, plus support during labor and delivery.

UT.summary: In Utah, Medicaid has covered doula care since April 1, 2026, including up to 8 hours of prenatal and postpartum visits and labor support; rates are listed only in the state's lookup tool.
UT.paymentNotes: Prenatal and postpartum support is billed in 15-minute units (T1032), limited to 32 units (8 hours) per rolling year. Labor support is one per-diem payment per pregnancy (T1033). Dollar rates are published only in Utah's online coverage and reimbursement lookup tool.
UT.certificationRequired: Enroll with Utah Medicaid via the Doula Provider Attestation: approved doula training plus 3 births in 5 years and CPR (certification pathway), or 10 births (5 in the last 2 years) plus 4 recommendation letters and CPR (experience pathway)
UT.notes: New benefit starting 4/1/2026 (SPA 25-0022, approved 12/19/2025). The state plan points to an online lookup tool for rates, so no total is given here. The 32-unit limit is one shared pool for prenatal and postpartum support, with no separate visit counts. Limits can be exceeded with prior authorization based on medical need. Telehealth is not allowed, and travel time and mileage are not covered. A Medicaid-enrolled qualified health professional must order doula services before they start, and the claim must include that provider's NPI. Limits apply per member, so seeing more than one doula does not add coverage. Utah Medicaid has no member page about doulas yet.

VT.summary: Vermont passed a 2025 law requiring Medicaid to cover certified doulas once federal approval comes through; it isn't paying yet.
VT.paymentNotes: No rates yet. Act 50 says it is the legislature's intent that DVHA pay 'reasonable and adequate' rates consistent with other states' Medicaid doula rates. Travel time and mileage are not reimbursable.
VT.certificationRequired: State certification as a community-based perinatal doula (Office of Professional Regulation, 26 V.S.A. ch. 84)
VT.notes: S.53 became Act 50, signed June 9, 2025. New law 33 V.S.A. § 1901n requires DVHA to reimburse certified community-based perinatal doulas for support during pregnancy, labor and delivery, and the postpartum period, regardless of pregnancy outcome. DVHA had to seek a state plan amendment by July 1, 2026. Medicaid coverage takes effect on the later of July 1, 2026 or SPA approval; we found no federal approval yet. The National Health Law Program expects a July 1, 2027 start. We found no DVHA doula page and no OPR doula certification page as of October 2026, even though the certification sections took effect July 1, 2026. The law requires paying for labor and delivery support.

VA.summary: In Virginia, Medicaid covers up to 8 prenatal or postpartum doula visits plus attendance at the birth, through 6 months after delivery; current dollar rates aren't published.
VA.paymentNotes: Visits are billed in 15-minute units: up to 6 units for the first prenatal visit and 4 units for each other visit, plus attendance at birth, and up to two value-based incentive payments (linkage to the mom's postpartum visit and the baby's pediatric visit). DMAS's 2022 doula flyer says Medicaid reimbursed $859 for 8 prenatal/postpartum visits and delivery, plus up to $100 in incentives. DMAS doesn't publish current doula rates; its fee files list the codes as individually priced.
VA.certificationRequired: Virginia state-certified community doula (Virginia Certification Board; 60 hours of VDH-approved training; $100 fee) plus $1M/$3M liability insurance to enroll
VA.notes: The National Health Law Program reports that a 2025 law (HB 1614) raises postpartum visits from 4 to 6 (10 total) and extends coverage to 12 months. DMAS's own doula page (checked Oct. 9, 2026) still says services are covered through 180 days after delivery. The approved SPA (21-0013) still allows 8 combined prenatal/postpartum visits, and we found no DMAS memo or SPA putting the expansion in place; 2026 bills HB 425 and HB 838 again address it. There's no current total: the only state dollar figure ($859) is from a 2022 flyer. The plan amendment is effective Jan. 1, 2022; DMAS said services would start in spring 2022. More than 8 visits, or services past 6 months after delivery, need service authorization. A mom needs a licensed practitioner's recommendation (DMAS-3100 form) before care starts; no prior authorization is needed otherwise. Most members are in Cardinal Care MCOs, and doulas must contract with each MCO.

WA.summary: In Washington, Medicaid covers doula care: up to $3,500 per pregnancy for an intake visit and up to 20 hours of prenatal and postpartum visits, plus support during labor and delivery.
WA.paymentNotes: $750 for one in-person prenatal intake visit of at least 2 hours (59899-U1), $750 flat for continuous in-person labor and delivery support (T1033), and $25 per 15 minutes (T1032) for up to 20 hours (80 units) of other prenatal and postpartum visits, of which 6 units are set aside for a comprehensive postpartum visit. Up to $3,500 per pregnancy. Fee schedule effective 1/1/2025.
WA.certificationRequired: Washington state-certified birth doula (Dept. of Health), NPI, and ProviderOne enrollment
WA.notes: Visits are time-based: one 20-hour (80-unit) pool for prenatal and postpartum support on top of the intake visit and labor support, with no fixed visit count. 6 units are reserved for a comprehensive postpartum visit and up to 74 units can go to either period. Limits can be extended case by case through HCA's limitation extension process. HCA's billing guide (effective 7/1/2026) does not cover audio-only telemedicine. HCA finalized permanent doula rules effective 8/25/2025. The National Health Law Program reports a statewide standing recommendation from HCA and DOH (October 2024) and coverage up to 12 months after pregnancy. HCA's doula page is aimed at providers; Apple Health has no member page about doulas.
